blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array `arr` of integers (positive, negative or zero), return the **length of the longest subarray** — a run of consecutive elements — whose sum is **0**. If there is none, return 0.

blocks.alt: The array 15, -2, 2, -8, 1, 7, 10, 23. The subarray -2, 2, -8, 1, 7 adds up to 0 and has length 5, the longest possible.

blocks.text: 1. Brute force: add up every subarray
Try every start i and every end j, add up `arr[i..j]` from scratch, and keep the longest one that sums to 0.
2. Optimal: a running sum for every start
`arr[i..j]` is just `arr[i..j − 1]` plus one more element, so keep a running sum while j moves right instead of starting over.
**Time O(n²), space O(1).** Good enough for small inputs — but n = 100,000 means 5 billion steps.
The key idea: the same prefix sum twice

Keep one running total from the start of the array — the **prefix sum**. Suppose the prefix sum at index b is x, and **later**, at index c, it is x **again**. Whatever came between b and c must have added up to nothing:

blocks.alt: A line from a to c. The sum from a to b is x and the sum from a to c is also x. Since sum(a..c) = sum(a..b) + sum(b..c), we get x = x + y, so y, the sum from b to c, is 0.

blocks.text: In the example, the prefix sum is **15** after index 0, and 15 **again** after index 2 and after index 5. So `arr[1..2]` and `arr[1..5]` both add up to 0. To get the **longest** such subarray at each index, pair it with the **earliest** spot where the same sum appeared.

blocks.alt: Prefix sums of 15, -2, 2, -8, 1, 7, 10, 23. Starting from 0 at index -1, they are 15, 13, 15, 7, 8, 15, 25, 48. The sum 15 appears at index 0 and again at index 5, so the elements at indexes 1 to 5 add up to 0: length 5 minus 0 = 5.

blocks.text: One more detail: a subarray that starts at **index 0** has no "earlier spot". Pretend there is one at index **−1** with prefix sum **0** — the empty start — so the map begins as `{0: −1}`.
3. Best solution: prefix sums + the first index of each sum

Walk once. Keep a map from **prefix sum → the first index it appeared at**. At each index: if the current sum is already in the map, the subarray after that index sums to 0 — update the best length. If it isn't, store it. **Never overwrite** an existing entry: the earliest index gives the longest subarray.

blocks.caption: The second row is the prefix sum after each index; the map keeps each sum's first index.

blocks.alt: The map after the walk: 0 to -1, 15 to 0, 13 to 1, 7 to 3, 8 to 4, then 25 and 48. At index 5 the sum 15 is found with index 0, so the length is 5 minus 0 = 5.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n)** — at most one map entry per index. (In Python the running total is named `total`, so it doesn't hide the built-in `sum`.)

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n³) time, O(1) space. Optimal: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Best: O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: **Starts at index 0** — `[1, -1, 5]`: the sum is 0 at index 1, matched by the `{0: −1}` entry: length 2. Forget that entry and you get 0.
**A single zero** — `[3, 0, 4]`: the sum repeats at once: length 1.
**Overwriting the first index** — `[1, -1, 1, -1]`: the answer is 4 only if sum 0 keeps index −1; storing the latest index would shrink it to 2.
**Largest Subarray of 0's and 1's** — count every 0 as −1 and this exact solution finds it. It's the next lesson.
**Longest subarray with sum k** — look up the first index of `sum − k` instead of `sum` (LeetCode's *Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k*).
**Is there any zero-sum subarray?** — a **set** of prefix sums is enough: return true at the first repeat.
**Count All Subarrays with Zero Sum** — store how many times each sum appeared, not where. Two lessons ahead.
